learn.canDo: Choose REST, GraphQL or gRPC for a caller and network, and spot the N+1 problem in GraphQL.
learn.why: API style is a standard design question. Tying the choice to the client and the network, not to fashion, is what interviewers look for.
learn.keyIdea: Match the style to the caller.

learn.canDo: Explain why offset pagination slows and drifts, and use cursor pagination on an indexed unique sort key.
learn.why: Deep offsets and repeated items are common production bugs. Cursor pagination is the expected answer.
learn.keyIdea: A cursor remembers the item, not a position.

learn.canDo: Specify what a server does with an idempotency key in each edge case: in flight, mismatched, failed, and cross-account.
learn.why: Adding a key is easy. The edge cases decide whether it works, and they are where follow-up questions go.

learn.canDo: Choose between URL versions, additive evolution and pinned versions, and size a deprecation window from client upgrade data.
learn.why: Breaking partners costs trust. A versioning plan with numbers shows maturity.
learn.keyIdea: You decide who pays for slow upgraders.

learn.canDo: Compare fixed window, token bucket and sliding window limiters on worst-case burst, rejection and memory.
learn.why: Rate limiter design is a staple interview case, and the boundary burst is the detail that separates answers.
learn.keyIdea: The window edge doubles a fixed limit.

learn.canDo: Compare polling, long polling, SSE and WebSockets on requests, delay and connection memory.
learn.why: Real-time features start with this choice. Quoting the cost of each shows you have run one.
learn.keyIdea: Polling spends effort on the question, not the answer.

learn.canDo: Design webhook delivery with long backoff, HMAC signing, timestamp checks and receiver-side dedup.
learn.why: Webhooks are the way most products integrate. Reliability and security are both on the checklist.
learn.keyIdea: A secret URL is obscure; a signature is the lock.

chapter.story: Pigeon opens up to partners and apps, and the team discovers how an API is a promise.
outcomes: Choose an API style by caller and network
Paginate and rate limit without surprises
Make requests safe to retry and changes safe to ship
Push events to clients and partners reliably and securely
chapter.why: An API is read by code you did not write and cannot update. Every shortcut shows up later as someone else's outage.
chapter.payoff: In an interview you can design an API and defend each choice. At work you will review one and know which promises it makes.
